P3Q1: Faith's object is the First Truth, known through revealed propositions rather than direct vision. Aquinas explains why the articles of faith are fixed, how they grew clearer over time, and why the Pope alone may formulate the Creed.
P3Q2: To believe is to assent with certainty to unseen truths on God's authority. Some truths must be believed explicitly by everyone, especially concerning Christ and the Trinity, and believing meritoriously engages both will and reason.
P3Q3: Confessing faith outwardly with the lips is itself an act of faith, flowing from the heart's inward belief. Such confession is necessary for salvation whenever silence would deny Christ or endanger the faith.
P3Q4: Faith is defined as the substance of things hoped for, residing in the intellect yet formed by charity. Lifeless faith lacking charity remains true faith, though it is the first and least certain of the virtues in one sense, most certain in another.
P3Q5: Faith existed differently in angels before their testing, is impossible in the damned demons despite forced belief, and admits of degrees among believers depending on certainty and readiness of will, though not all articles can be rejected while retaining faith.
P3Q6: Faith, whether living or lifeless, is caused in man by God's infusion through grace, not acquired by natural reason or human teaching alone, since it exceeds what unaided reason can prove.
P3Q7: Faith produces effects including a certain servile or filial fear of God and, when informed by charity, purifies the heart from earthly attachments and error by directing the soul to unseen truth.
P3Q8: The gift of understanding is a supernatural light of the Holy Ghost enabling penetration into revealed truths beyond bare faith; it is speculative and practical, given to all in grace, and answers to the beatitude of the clean of heart.
P3Q9: The gift of knowledge rightly judges about created things in reference to God, guarding against error in matters of faith and directing conduct; it corresponds to the beatitude of those who mourn over sin.
P3Q10: Unbelief, a sin of the intellect refusing revealed truth, is graver among those who once knew the faith than among pagans. Aquinas treats disputation, toleration of unbelievers' rites, and forced baptism of Jewish children.
P3Q11: Heresy is a species of unbelief that selectively rejects articles of Christian faith while retaining others; obstinate heretics should not be tolerated and may be punished, though the Church readily receives those who repent.
P3Q12: Apostasy from the faith is a grave species of unbelief; a ruler who apostatizes may forfeit the allegiance of Christian subjects, since authority over the faithful presupposes fidelity to the Church.
P3Q13: Blasphemy, speaking evil against God's goodness, opposes the confession of faith and is always a mortal sin, among the gravest sins, and one into which the damned in hell inevitably fall.
P3Q14: The unforgivable sin against the Holy Ghost is malicious rejection of the very remedies of sin, distinguished into six kinds such as despair and impenitence; it is forgivable in this life only through God's mercy overcoming obstinacy.
P3Q15: Blindness of mind and dulness of sense, which impede grasping spiritual truth, are sins rooted in inordinate attachment to worldly things, especially the sins of the flesh that cloud judgment.
P3Q16: The Old Law fittingly contained precepts commanding faith in God and forbidding false worship, along with precepts fostering the exercise of knowledge and understanding needed to know and serve God rightly.
P3Q17: Hope is a theological virtue whose proper object is eternal happiness attained through God's help; it can extend to hoping for others' salvation and lawfully trusting human aid, and follows faith while preceding perfect charity.
P3Q18: Hope resides in the will, is absent from the blessed who already possess happiness and from the damned who cannot attain it, yet the wayfarer's hope carries genuine certainty grounded in God's power and mercy.
P3Q19: Fear of God is fitting and divided into filial, initial, servile, and worldly fear; servile fear of punishment can coexist with charity, while filial fear of offending God remains even in heaven, corresponding to poverty of spirit.
P3Q20: Despair is a mortal sin of abandoning hope in God's mercy, distinct from unbelief though often accompanying it, and it is among the gravest sins because it removes the very motive for turning back to God; it arises chiefly from sloth.
P3Q21: Presumption is sinfully trusting excessively in one's own power or in God's mercy without due effort; it is more directly opposed to fear than to hope and springs from vainglory.
P3Q22: Divine law fittingly commands hope in God for salvation and fear of offending Him, since these affections must be directed by precept to keep man properly disposed toward his final end.
P3Q23: Charity is a supernatural friendship with God based on shared beatitude, infused into the soul as a virtue distinct from and more excellent than all others, the very form giving life and merit to every virtuous act.
P3Q24: Charity resides in the will, is infused by God apart from natural capacity, and can increase indefinitely through repeated acts toward its perfection in heaven; it is lost entirely through a single mortal sin.
P3Q25: Charity's love extends beyond God to neighbor, self, one's own body, sinners, enemies, and even the angels, though not to demons, since love of neighbor for God's sake is inseparable from love of God.
P3Q26: Charity observes a rational order: God is loved most, then oneself spiritually, then neighbor, with closer kin and greater friends loved variously depending on the good in question; this order of love persists in heaven.
P3Q27: The chief act of charity is to love, understood as willing good to another out of union with God; God must be loved for His own sake and, ideally, without measure, and loving God exceeds loving neighbor in merit.
P3Q28: Spiritual joy in God is an effect of charity, compatible with concurrent sorrow over sin or affliction, and can grow toward its fullness, though joy itself is an effect rather than a distinct virtue.
P3Q29: Peace, more than mere concord, is the tranquility of order following upon charity's harmony of desires; all things naturally desire it, and it is charity's proper effect rather than a separate virtue.
P3Q30: Mercy is sorrow for another's distress as one's own, arising from a felt kinship in weakness; it is a genuine virtue when regulated by reason and, uniquely, is among the greatest since it gives from one's own abundance to another's need.
P3Q31: Beneficence, doing good to others, is an act flowing from charity owed to all but especially to those closer to us; while charity commands it generally, beneficence itself is not a wholly separate virtue.
P3Q32: Almsgiving, an act of charity and mercy expressed materially or spiritually, is commanded by precept though its measure is left to discretion; corporal alms may be given even from necessities in true need, but never from ill-gotten goods.
P3Q33: Fraternal correction, admonishing a sinning neighbor for his amendment, is an act of charity binding on all under precept, not only prelates, though correction of one's own prelate and public denunciation follow a due order beginning with private admonition.
P3Q34: Hatred, willing evil to another, cannot be directed at God as He is in Himself but only at what opposes one's desires in Him, making it a most grievous sin; hatred of neighbor is likewise sinful and can spring from envy.
P3Q35: Sloth is sorrow at the spiritual good within, a real and sometimes mortal sin distinct from mere laziness, ranked among the capital vices because it drives the soul away from charity's demands.
P3Q36: Envy is sorrow at another's good regarded as diminishing one's own excellence; it is a sin, mortal in its complete form, and reckoned a capital vice that spawns further sins against neighbor.
P3Q37: Discord, a refusal to agree in will with others on matters of good, opposes the peace charity produces and is a sin that Aquinas traces to the root vice of vainglory.
P3Q38: Contention, quarrelsome disputing marked by disorderly zeal rather than truth-seeking, is a mortal sin when it involves grave disrespect, and like discord it proceeds from the desire for vainglory.
P3Q39: Schism, willful separation from ecclesial unity or from submission to the Pope, is a distinct grave sin, in some respects worse than unbelief, and schismatics rightly lose spiritual authority and merit excommunication.
P3Q40: War is not inherently sinful when waged by proper authority, for just cause, and right intention, though ambushes are permissible while fighting on holy days and clerical combat require special justification.
P3Q41: Strife, unregulated private combat or brawling, is generally sinful when it breaches due order or charity, and Aquinas traces it as a daughter vice arising from anger.
P3Q42: Sedition, stirring discord and division within a community against legitimate authority, is a distinct mortal sin against the common good, separate from ordinary strife or war between individuals.
P3Q43: Scandal is word or deed that occasions another's spiritual downfall; it is generally sinful, though the perfect may sometimes give occasion for others' weak scandal, and neither spiritual nor, ordinarily, temporal goods should be sacrificed merely to avoid it.
P3Q44: Charity requires precepts commanding love of God above all and of neighbor as oneself; loving God with whole heart, soul, and strength is fulfillable imperfectly in this life, and the order of charity is implicitly included in the command.
P3Q45: Wisdom as a gift of the Holy Ghost judges divine things through connatural union with God, is both speculative and practical, present in all who have grace, and answers to the beatitude of the peacemakers.
P3Q46: Folly, an insensibility to spiritual and divine goods opposed to the gift of wisdom, is a genuine sin that Aquinas links to the corrupting influence of lust dulling right judgment.
P3Q47: Prudence, right reason applied to action, is an intellectual virtue in the practical reason that appoints the end and finds the means for moral virtue, commanding action, extending to governance of others, yet absent in the wicked and lost through neglect.
P3Q48: Prudence is fittingly divided into memory of the past, understanding of the present, and foresight of the future, the three parts required for sound practical judgment and command.
P3Q49: The integral parts enabling prudent action include memory, understanding, docility, shrewdness, reason, foresight, circumspection, and caution, each contributing a distinct element needed for well-ordered practical judgment.
P3Q50: Prudence takes specific forms suited to different domains of governance: regnative for rulers, political for citizens, domestic for household management, and military for the conduct of war, each a distinct species of the one virtue.
P3Q51: Allied to prudence are euboulia, the virtue of deliberating well, and synesis and gnome, virtues of sound judgment according to common and exceptional cases respectively, each a distinct habit perfecting practical reasoning.
P3Q52: Counsel, a gift of the Holy Ghost, perfects prudence by disposing man to be readily guided by God in particular actions; it endures even in heaven in a transformed way and answers to the beatitude of the merciful.
P3Q53: Imprudence is a distinct sin opposed to prudence, including precipitation, thoughtlessness, and inconstancy, vices that undermine sound deliberation and judgment and are traced to the disordering influence of lust.
P3Q54: Negligence, a special sin opposed to the diligence required by prudence, is failing to apply due care in one's duties, and can be mortal when it involves neglect of something gravely obligatory.
P3Q55: Certain vices counterfeit prudence: carnal prudence serving the flesh, craftiness, guile, and fraud in seeking ends by false means, and excessive worldly solicitude, all traced ultimately to covetousness.
P3Q56: Divine law fittingly includes precepts commanding prudence and forbidding its counterfeit vices, ensuring that practical wisdom is directed toward God and the true good rather than deceit or worldly cunning.
P3Q57: Right, the object of justice, is what is due to another; it divides into natural right, grounded in nature itself, and positive right, established by human or divine enactment, with the right of nations classed under natural right broadly considered.
P3Q58: Justice is the constant will to render each his due; it is a virtue seated in the will, directed toward others, and while general justice concerns the common good, particular justice regulates individual exchanges and distributions.
P3Q59: Injustice is a special vice of willingly withholding another's due; one becomes unjust by unjust acts, and though injustice can sometimes be suffered willingly without wrong to oneself, every unjust act is a mortal sin absolutely considered.
P3Q60: Judgment, the act of justice applying the law to a case, is lawful when made by proper authority according to right reason and evidence, but sinful when based on rash suspicion or usurped authority.
P3Q61: Justice divides into distributive justice, apportioning common goods proportionally, and commutative justice, governing equal exchange between individuals; each observes a different kind of mean, and simple retaliation is not strictly identical with the just.
P3Q62: Restitution, restoring what was unjustly taken or its equivalent, is an act of commutative justice necessary for salvation whenever another's due has been violated, binding the taker and, in some cases, others who benefited, and generally owed without delay.
P3Q63: Respect of persons, unjustly favoring someone for extraneous qualities rather than merit, is sinful especially in distributing spiritual goods, in honors, and gravely so in judicial sentences where impartiality is required.
P3Q64: Killing an innocent human being is always unlawful, but public authority may justly execute grave sinners for the common good; private self-defense causing death is permissible when death is not directly intended, while suicide and killing by accident raise further distinct questions.
P3Q65: Other bodily injuries such as maiming, corporal punishment by parents or masters, and imprisonment can be lawful when exercised with due authority and moderation, though such injuries are aggravated when done to persons under another's special care.
P3Q66: Possessing external goods as one's own is not against natural law though common use remains an ideal; theft, secretly taking another's property, and robbery, taking it violently, are distinct mortal sins, though theft committed from extreme necessity may be excused.
P3Q67: A judge sins by exceeding his jurisdiction, by ruling against known truth despite contrary evidence, by condemning without accusation, and by improperly remitting due punishment, since judicial justice requires fidelity to truth and law.
P3Q68: Just accusation requires proper written form and honest intention, since calumny, collusion, or evasion corrupt it; an accuser who fails to prove his charge is liable to suffer the very penalty he sought to inflict.
P3Q69: A defendant may lawfully deny facts that would lead to unjust self-condemnation but not use actual calumny; appealing a judgment to escape it is permissible, though one condemned justly to death may not forcibly resist execution.
P3Q70: Witnesses are generally bound to give truthful evidence when duly required, and the testimony of two or three credible persons ordinarily suffices; unjust rejection of evidence and giving false witness are serious violations of justice, mortal sins.
P3Q71: An advocate is bound in some circumstances to defend the poor without fee, may be lawfully barred from practice for certain defects, sins by knowingly defending an unjust cause, and may licitly accept a fee for honest legal service.
P3Q72: Reviling, insulting another to his dishonor by injurious words, is generally a mortal sin though sometimes venial by lack of gravity, is best patiently endured, and typically springs from unchecked anger.
P3Q73: Backbiting, secretly ruining another's reputation through words, is a mortal sin, indeed among the most grievous sins against neighbor since it robs the good name a man may value more than material goods; listeners who tolerate it also sin.
P3Q74: Tale-bearing, sowing discord by relaying disparaging reports between parties to break their friendship, is a distinct sin from backbiting and generally judged less grave than outright detraction.
P3Q75: Derision, mocking another's faults or shortcomings to shame him, is a special sin distinct from reviling or backbiting, and can become mortal when it inflicts serious contempt or injury on its object.
P3Q76: Cursing, invoking evil upon someone, is lawful only when rightly directed as a form of just judgment or exhortation; cursing an irrational creature is only figuratively meaningful, and malicious cursing is a mortal sin, though less grave than backbiting.
P3Q77: Selling above just price is unlawful, as is concealing substantial defects in goods sold since the seller owes truthful disclosure; reselling at a markup can be licit when justified by expense, risk, or added value.
P3Q78: Usury, charging a price for the mere use of money lent, is intrinsically unjust since it sells what does not exist separately from the money itself; ill-gotten usurious profit must be restored, and borrowing under usurious terms is a distinct question of lesser culpability.
P3Q79: Justice as a whole comprises declining evil and doing good; failing a positive duty (omission) and violating a prohibition (transgression) are distinct kinds of sin, with omission of grave duty sometimes reckoned even more serious.
P3Q80: Numerous potential parts, or annexed virtues, attach to justice, extending its concern for due order beyond strict debt into religion, piety, observance, truth, gratitude, and related virtues, fittingly enumerated according to their partial resemblance to justice.
P3Q81: Religion is the virtue directing man to render due worship to God alone; it is a single, special virtue, not itself theological but the greatest of the moral virtues, expressed through both interior devotion and external acts.
P3Q82: Devotion, the will's readiness to serve God promptly, is the principal interior act of religion, caused chiefly by contemplating God's goodness and our own insufficiency, and naturally issues in spiritual joy despite occasional accompanying sorrow.
P3Q83: Prayer, an act of reason directed by the will and belonging properly to religion, should be addressed to God, may rightly request specific and even temporal goods, be offered for others including enemies, and is meritorious when made attentively and perseveringly.
P3Q84: Adoration, an act of religion expressing reverent submission to God, involves both interior submission and fitting bodily gestures, though it does not strictly require any particular place.
P3Q85: Sacrifice, offering something to God in acknowledgment of His sovereignty, belongs to the natural law and to religion alone as its object, though not every individual is bound personally to offer it under all circumstances.
P3Q86: Oblations and first-fruits, offerings to God from one's goods, are due in some form under natural precept, primarily support the clergy and the divine cult, and may be made from anything one lawfully possesses.
P3Q87: Payment of tithes to support the clergy is obligatory as a matter of precept extending in principle to all lawful goods, and even clergy who possess property of their own owe tithes in certain cases.
P3Q88: A vow, a deliberate promise made to God, must concern a better good to be valid; while binding once made, entering vows is generally praiseworthy, solemnized notably by religious profession, and admits dispensation or commutation by proper authority.
P3Q89: An oath, calling God to witness the truth of an assertion, is lawful when marked by truth, judgment, and justice, carries strong binding force even exceeding a simple vow, though it can be voided by certain conditions of person or circumstance.
P3Q90: Adjuration, invoking God's name to command another, is lawful when directed at rational creatures for good ends and even at demons for licit purposes, but not meaningfully applied to irrational creatures incapable of obedience.
P3Q91: Praising God vocally and through song is fitting, since exterior words and music arouse and express interior devotion, stirring the mind to greater reverence and love of God.
P3Q92: Superstition is a vice opposed to religion by excess, offering worship in an undue manner, undue object, or undue mode, and takes various species such as idolatry, divination, and improper observances.
P3Q93: Even worship of the true God can become superstitious and pernicious when offered in an improper manner, time, or with additions not sanctioned by the Church, constituting an excess opposed to right religion.
P3Q94: Idolatry, offering divine worship to a creature or image, is a species of superstition and among the gravest sins since it most directly denies God's due honor, arising from human error, passion, and demonic deception.
P3Q95: Divination, seeking hidden knowledge through illicit means, is sinful superstition in its many forms, including invoking demons, false astrology claiming to determine free acts, interpreting dreams, omens, and casting lots for improper ends.
P3Q96: Superstitious observances such as magical practices, charms for physical alteration, or fortune-telling rituals are unlawful, since they seek effects through implicit demonic pacts rather than natural causes or divine power; wearing divine words devoutly may be permissible.
P3Q97: Tempting God, presuming to test His power or providence through needless deeds expecting a special outcome, is sinful, opposed to religion, and in some respects more grievous than ordinary superstition.
P3Q98: Perjury, swearing falsely or breaking a sworn oath, requires a false or violated assertion under oath, is always sinful, generally mortally so, and even one who knowingly induces such an oath shares the guilt.
P3Q99: Sacrilege, the violation of something consecrated to God—persons, places, or things—is a distinct grave sin whose species vary according to the sacred object profaned, traditionally subject to punishment.
P3Q100: Simony, the deliberate intention to buy or sell spiritual things or things annexed to them, is always sinful; payment purely for licit related services may be permissible, and those guilty are fittingly deprived of what they wrongly acquired.
P3Q101: Piety, rendering due honor to parents, country, and those connected by kinship, is a distinct virtue from religion, though duties of piety must sometimes yield precedence to the higher demands of religion toward God.
P3Q102: Observance, paying honor and worship to persons of excellence and dignity such as superiors, is a distinct virtue related to but lesser than piety, since piety concerns closer natural bonds.
P3Q103: Dulia, honor rendered to excellent human persons, particularly the saints, is distinct from latria which is due to God alone, and admits various degrees corresponding to differing dignity.
P3Q104: Obedience to legitimate superiors is generally owed by inferiors, forming a distinct virtue, though not the greatest since it depends on charity; obedience to God is unconditional, but obedience to human authority yields where commands conflict with divine law.
P3Q105: Disobedience to legitimate precepts is a mortal sin when it involves contempt or grave matter, though it is not reckoned the most grievous of sins overall.
P3Q106: Thankfulness, or gratitude, owed to benefactors including God, is a distinct virtue requiring recognition and timely repayment proportioned to the benefactor's disposition, and ideally the response should exceed the favor received.
P3Q107: Ingratitude, failing to acknowledge or repay a benefit received, is always at least a venial sin, sometimes mortal, and constitutes a distinct vice that can justify withholding future favors from the persistently ungrateful.
P3Q108: Vengeance, inflicting punishment on a wrongdoer, is lawful when exercised by proper authority with right intention for correction or the common good, using customary means, though it should not fall on the involuntarily sinning.
P3Q109: Truthfulness, manifesting oneself as one truly is in word and deed, is a distinct virtue annexed to justice, generally inclining toward understatement rather than exaggeration of one's own worth.
P3Q110: Lying, speaking contrary to what one holds true with intent to deceive, always opposes truth and is sinful, divided into helpful, jesting, and malicious lies, though not every lie is equally a mortal sin.
P3Q111: Dissimulation, feigning what is not true through action, is generally sinful, and hypocrisy, a species of dissimulation feigning virtue or holiness one lacks, opposes truth and can be a mortal sin depending on intent and matter.
P3Q112: Boasting, exaggerating one's own qualities beyond the truth, is opposed to the virtue of truth and, depending on intent and effect, can be a mortal sin.
P3Q113: Irony, understating oneself beneath the truth, is a lesser sin against truthfulness than boasting, since deficiency in self-praise is less disordered than excess.
P3Q114: Friendliness or affability, behaving agreeably toward others in social intercourse, is a distinct virtue related to justice, moderating truthful and pleasant conduct toward all in daily dealings.
P3Q115: Flattery, insincere praise aimed at pleasing rather than truth, is a sin opposed to affability, and can become mortal when it leads another into serious wrongdoing or scandal.
P3Q116: Quarreling, contentiously opposing others in speech contrary to affability, is a sin generally considered more grievous than flattery because it directly and offensively injures social harmony.
P3Q117: Liberality, the virtuous use and giving of material wealth according to right reason, is a genuine virtue centered on money's use, especially giving, though it is not classified strictly as a part of justice nor the greatest virtue.
P3Q118: Covetousness, an inordinate desire for wealth, is a distinct sin opposed to liberality, mortal when it violates justice, and reckoned a capital vice generating treachery, fraud, and other allied sins.
P3Q119: Prodigality, excessive and disordered spending, is opposed to covetousness though generally judged a lesser sin, since it errs through excessive generosity rather than injustice toward others.
P3Q120: Epikeia, or equity, the virtue of interpreting law according to the lawgiver's true intent in unforeseen cases, is a genuine virtue and a higher part of justice guiding right application of positive law.
P3Q121: Piety as a gift of the Holy Ghost renders worship and duty to God as universal Father with filial affection; it corresponds to the second beatitude, blessed are the meek, softening harshness toward God and neighbor.
P3Q122: The precepts of the Decalogue are precepts of justice ordering man to God and neighbor; each commandment, from worship of one God through honoring parents to the final six precepts, is fittingly expressed for its purpose.
P3Q123: Fortitude is the virtue moderating fear and daring especially amid mortal danger, most perfectly in battle; its chief act is steadfast endurance rather than attack, and it ranks as a cardinal virtue, though not the highest.
P3Q124: Martyrdom, voluntarily enduring death for truth or virtue's sake, is an act of the greatest perfection of fortitude informed by charity; death for the faith is its most proper cause, though other virtues can also occasion true martyrdom.
P3Q125: Fear, an excessive shrinking from danger that abandons duty, is a sin contrary to fortitude, mortal when it leads one to forsake a grave obligation, though extreme fear can sometimes mitigate culpability.
P3Q126: Fearlessness, a defective lack of due fear even where fear would be reasonable, is itself a vice opposed to fortitude by deficiency, differing from the virtuous control of fear that fortitude requires.
P3Q127: Daring, rushing rashly into danger without due deliberation, is a vice opposed to fortitude by excess, contrasting with the virtue's tempered courage guided by reason.
P3Q128: The parts of fortitude include the principal acts of confidence and patient endurance, along with allied virtues such as magnanimity, magnificence, patience, and perseverance, each contributing an aspect of courageous constancy.
P3Q129: Magnanimity is the virtue of pursuing great honor becomingly, a genuine special virtue and part of fortitude, involving well-grounded confidence and security, though it properly uses rather than depends on fortune's goods.
P3Q130: Presumption, aspiring to honors or achievements beyond one's due capacity, is a sin opposed to magnanimity by excess, disregarding the true limits of one's ability.
P3Q131: Ambition, an inordinate desire for honor or advancement, is a sin opposed to magnanimity by excess, seeking recognition disproportionate to genuine merit or beyond due order.
P3Q132: Vainglory, desiring empty or ill-founded glory, is sinful and opposed to magnanimity, mortal in serious matter, ranked a capital vice generating daughters like boasting, hypocrisy, and discord.
P3Q133: Pusillanimity, shrinking from undertaking good works proportionate to one's capacity out of excessive self-distrust, is a sin opposed to magnanimity by deficiency, failing to pursue the great good one is fit for.
P3Q134: Magnificence, the virtue of achieving something great through substantial and fitting expenditure, is a special virtue and part of fortitude, distinct from ordinary liberality by the scale of its undertaking.
P3Q135: Meanness, a defect opposed to magnificence through insufficient or inappropriate spending on great works, is a vice, though the corresponding excess is less clearly identified as a distinct vice.
P3Q136: Patience, enduring hardship and sorrow without succumbing to disordered sadness, is a genuine virtue requiring grace to be perfect, classified as a part of fortitude, and closely allied with longanimity in bearing long delay.
P3Q137: Perseverance, steadfast continuance in good despite difficulty over time, is a virtue and part of fortitude, encompassing constancy against external obstacles, and its completion in final perseverance requires special divine help.
P3Q138: Effeminacy, giving up too easily under difficulty or the lure of pleasure, and pertinacity, obstinately persisting beyond reason, are the opposed vices flanking the virtue of perseverance.
P3Q139: Fortitude as a gift of the Holy Ghost strengthens the soul with confidence to overcome grave dangers through reliance on God's help, corresponding to the beatitude of those who hunger and thirst for justice.
P3Q140: Divine law fittingly contains precepts commanding fortitude itself and precepts for its allied virtues, ensuring courage and steadfastness are properly ordered toward God and the common good.
P3Q141: Temperance is the cardinal virtue moderating desire and pleasure, especially of touch and taste connected with self-preservation and procreation, regulated according to what right reason and the needs of life require.
P3Q142: Insensibility, a deficient lack of due pleasure in necessary things, is a vice opposed to temperance, generally rarer than intemperance, which especially disgraces reason by subjecting it to bodily pleasure like a child.
P3Q143: Temperance comprises several parts including shamefacedness, honesty, and virtues such as abstinence, sobriety, and chastity governing specific pleasures, each moderating a particular aspect of desire.
P3Q144: Shamefacedness, a fitting fear of disgrace from base action, is a praiseworthy passion akin to virtue, felt more acutely before those closest to us, and can even affect virtuous persons regarding lesser faults.
P3Q145: Honesty, the moral beauty attaching to virtuous conduct, is closely allied with virtue itself though formally distinct, differing from the merely useful or pleasant, and is reckoned a part of temperance.
P3Q146: Abstinence, moderate restraint in food, is a distinct special virtue subordinate to temperance, disciplining the desire for eating according to right reason and higher spiritual purposes.
P3Q147: Fasting, voluntarily restricting food as an act of virtue and religious discipline, is a matter of Church precept binding those able, traditionally observed with one meal and abstinence from meat, though exact practices vary.
P3Q148: Gluttony, inordinate desire in eating, is a sin, mortal in its full form though sometimes venial, reckoned a capital vice with six identifiable species and daughters that dull the mind and excite other vices.
P3Q149: Sobriety, moderation especially regarding intoxicating drink, is a special virtue distinct from temperance in general; the use of wine itself is not unlawful, though greater sobriety is expected of those in positions of responsibility.
P3Q150: Drunkenness, voluntarily impairing reason through excessive drink, is a mortal sin when knowingly incurred, among the graver sins of intemperance, though involuntary intoxication may excuse or diminish other resulting sins.
P3Q151: Chastity, moderating venereal pleasure according to right reason, is a special virtue distinct from abstinence, with purity most closely associated with the cleanness it preserves in body and mind.
P3Q152: Virginity, integrity of the flesh preserved by perpetual resolve, is lawful and a genuine virtue when embraced for spiritual motives; consecrated virginity surpasses marriage in excellence, though it is not absolutely the greatest of all virtues.
P3Q153: Lust, disordered desire for venereal pleasure, concerns acts that are not inherently sinful within marriage but become sinful outside right order; it is a capital vice generating numerous daughter vices that darken the mind.
P3Q154: Lust's species include simple fornication, mortal though sometimes judged less grave than other sins against neighbor, along with seduction, rape, adultery, incest, sacrilege, and the unnatural vice, which Aquinas judges the gravest species since it most violates nature's order.
P3Q155: Continence, resisting strong contrary desires of the flesh through effort of will, is a praiseworthy but imperfect virtue residing chiefly in the will overcoming the concupiscible appetite, ranked below full temperance which experiences no such struggle.
P3Q156: Incontinence, yielding to passion against one's better judgment, pertains to the soul's rational failure rather than mere bodily weakness; it is sinful, generally less grave than settled intemperance, though incontinence in anger is judged worse than in desire.
P3Q157: Clemency, moderating punishment, and meekness, restraining anger's excess, though related, are formally distinct virtues, and both are genuine though not the greatest virtues overall.
P3Q158: Anger, a passion for just retribution, is not inherently sinful and can be lawful when moderate and reasonable; but excessive or misdirected anger is sinful, sometimes mortally, ranked a capital vice with several species and daughters, opposed also by a defective lack of anger.
P3Q159: Cruelty, taking harsh pleasure in inflicting excessive punishment, is opposed to clemency and differs from savage brutality, which delights in causing suffering without even the pretext of just retribution.
P3Q160: Modesty moderates less central movements and appearances, forming a genuine part of temperance that governs not only interior desires but outward comportment as well.
P3Q161: Humility, moderating inordinate self-esteem through recognition of one's own deficiency before God, is a genuine virtue of the appetite rather than mere self-abasement before all men equally; though not the greatest virtue, its traditional twelve degrees fittingly express its practice.
P3Q162: Pride, inordinate desire for one's own excellence and honor, is a special mortal sin seated in the irascible faculty, taking four principal species; it is the gravest sin in a sense and reckoned the root of the first sin and a capital vice.
P3Q163: Adam's first sin was pride, specifically coveting a likeness to God's excellence not owed him; committed with fuller knowledge and freedom than Eve's, it was more grievous than any sin since, given the perfection of his original state.
P3Q164: Death and accompanying miseries are the fitting punishment for original sin, and Scripture's specific curses on Adam, Eve, and the serpent correspond appropriately to the nature and circumstances of their transgression.
P3Q165: It was fitting that our first parents be tempted by the devil to test and manifest their freedom, and the actual manner and progressive order of the temptation, working through the weaker party first, was fittingly arranged.
P3Q166: Studiousness, the virtue moderating desire to know, focuses properly on regulating the pursuit of knowledge according to right order, and is classed as a part of temperance restraining disordered curiosity.
P3Q167: Curiosity, an inordinate desire for knowledge pursued for wrong motives or in improper matters, can afflict both intellectual inquiry and sensory experience, constituting a vice opposed to studiousness.
P3Q168: Certain virtues govern outward bodily movement and demeanor, including moderation in play, since fitting recreation is virtuous, while both excessive playfulness and a graceless lack of all mirth can be sinful extremes.
P3Q169: Virtue and vice can attach to one's outward apparel insofar as it reflects and affects the soul's disposition; ordinary feminine adornment for legitimate purposes is not inherently a mortal sin, though vanity or seduction through dress can be.
P3Q170: Divine law fittingly establishes precepts of temperance itself and of its annexed virtues, directing the moderation of pleasure and desire toward properly ordered ends under God's law.
P3Q171: Prophecy is a form of supernatural knowledge, a transient divine gift rather than a permanent habit, chiefly concerned with future contingent events revealed by God beyond the prophet's natural power to know.
P3Q172: Prophecy cannot arise from purely natural causes but comes through angelic mediation from God; while a suitable natural disposition and virtuous life ordinarily assist it, prophetic-like foreknowledge can also proceed, in limited and lesser ways, from demons.
P3Q173: Prophets do not see the divine essence directly in ordinary prophecy but receive either new impressed intelligible forms or an intensified light of judgment; prophetic vision, often accompanied by withdrawal from the senses, need not exhaust full comprehension of what is revealed.
P3Q174: Prophecy is fittingly divided by degree into predestination, foreknowledge, and denunciation; visions joined with imaginative representation, though still ranked below pure intellectual vision, especially exalt Moses as the greatest prophet, with degrees varying across salvation history.
P3Q175: Rapture is the soul's forcible elevation to divine things surpassing ordinary connatural knowing, pertaining chiefly to the cognitive power; in Paul's rapture he glimpsed the divine essence while withdrawn from bodily senses, though whether his soul was fully separated remained uncertain even to him.
P3Q176: The gift of tongues bestowed at Pentecost enabled the apostles to speak in every language needed for evangelization, a grace considered less excellent overall than the gift of prophecy itself.
P3Q177: Gratuitous graces attach to speech, including the word of wisdom and knowledge enabling effective instruction of others in divine truth, a grace that can fittingly be granted even to women for private, though not public teaching.
P3Q178: The gratuitous grace of working miracles, exceeding the ordinary course of nature to confirm doctrine, can even be exercised by the wicked as an instrumental gift, distinct from personal sanctity.
P3Q179: Human life is fittingly divided into the active life, occupied with external works, and the contemplative life, occupied chiefly with the truth, an adequate division corresponding to the two basic orientations of rational activity.
P3Q180: The contemplative life centers on the intellect's loving gaze upon truth, especially divine truth, aided by the moral virtues that free it from disturbance; it cannot in this life reach the vision of God's essence, yet yields genuine delight though not uninterrupted continuity.
P3Q181: The active life engages the moral virtues in external works for others' good, including teaching insofar as it flows from contemplation; prudence directs it, and something of ordered activity is thought to remain even after this life.
P3Q182: Considered absolutely the contemplative life is more excellent since it concerns God directly, yet the active life of teaching and preaching, which communicates the fruits of contemplation, can be more meritorious and generally must precede contemplation in the soul's ascent.
P3Q183: The Church rightly contains varied duties and states corresponding to differing offices, actions, and degrees of spiritual progress, from beginners through those advancing to those already perfect.
P3Q184: The perfection of Christian life consists chiefly in charity, attainable only relatively in this life; it lies principally in observing the commandments while the counsels serve as aids, and formal states of perfection belong properly to religious and bishops who bind themselves to strive for it.
P3Q185: Desiring the episcopal office for right motives is not unlawful, though one may sometimes refuse it; a bishop should excel in virtue, generally may not abandon his flock for religious life or persecution, may retain modest personal property, and sins gravely by withholding Church goods from the poor.
P3Q186: Religious life properly consists in binding oneself by vow to the counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience under a rule; obedience is the chief of the three vows, and religious sin more gravely than seculars committing the same faults due to their heightened obligation.
P3Q187: Religious may lawfully teach, preach, engage in some secular business when needed, and live on alms or beg according to their rule, though manual labor is not always strictly obligatory and coarser dress is fittingly permitted as a sign of poverty.
P3Q188: Religious orders rightly take diverse forms directed to active works like preaching, teaching, or care of the sick, or to the contemplative life, which is generally most excellent; possessing goods in common does not itself diminish perfection, and community life is generally judged more perfect than solitary life.
P3Q189: Entering religious life is praiseworthy even without prior lengthy practice of virtue since the religious state itself aids growth in it; children, parish priests, and those bound by prior vow have specific conditions, and prompt entry without excessive deliberation is commended.
